## Lithosphere and Plate Motion
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they mark the boundaries where tectonic plates interact. The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere, moving via mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push at rates measured in centimetres per year. At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, causing normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Stress builds when plate edges lock by friction, until strain exceeds rock strength, releasing as earthquakes. Fault geometry, rheological contrasts, and curved margins also focus deformation.
Key points: Earthquakes trace plate interactions; lithosphere is rigid plates on asthenosphere; motion is cm/yr; stress accumulation from locked edges. Questions: Why are earthquakes not random? What happens at divergent boundaries? How is plate motion measured? What causes stress accumulation?

## Types of Plate Boundaries
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they outline the moving plates' framework. The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere, moving at centimetres per year. At boundaries, plates interact in three ways: divergent (pulling apart, causing normal-fault quakes at shallow depths), convergent (colliding, causing thrust-fault quakes from deep to shallow), and transform (sliding past, causing strike-slip quakes at shallow to intermediate depths).
Quakes cluster at boundaries because plate edges lock by friction, building strain until it exceeds rock strength. Fault geometry, rheological contrasts, and curved margins also focus deformation. So, the pattern of earthquakes directly reflects plate kinematics.

## Plate Speed and Earthquake Frequency
Faster plate motion means more frequent large earthquakes. The Pacific Plate moves at about 5 cm/yr, and the Nazca Plate at about 8 cm/yr; these speeds drive the high frequency of large quakes along the Ring of Fire.
Earthquake depths vary by setting: shallow events (≤10 km) dominate divergent ridges and transform faults, while intermediate-to-deep events (30–300 km) occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone of subducting slabs. A typical subduction quake at 30 km depth releases energy from both crustal bending and slab dehydration.
The seismic cycle at a convergent margin has four phases: interseismic (strain accumulates, decades to centuries), coseismic (sudden slip releases energy, seconds to minutes), postseismic (afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation, months to years), and preseismic (possible foreshocks or slow slip).
Seismic gap theory says segments that have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events. GPS and InSAR monitor plate-scale velocities (cm/yr) to refine coupling models.

## Double-Entry Bookkeeping Fundamentals
Double-entry bookkeeping records every financial transaction in at least two accounts, ensuring the books always balance. The golden rule is that for every debit, there must be an equal and offsetting credit.
To record a transaction, first identify it: determine if cash is moving in or out and which category it belongs to (e.g., inventory purchase, sales revenue, rent expense). Then determine the two accounts affected—for example, paying for inventory with cash affects the 'Inventory' asset account and the 'Cash' asset account.
Apply the debit and credit rules using the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity): debits increase assets and expenses; credits increase liabilities, equity, and revenue. Finally, record the entry with the date, a description, the debit amount, and the credit amount in the general ledger, and verify that total debits equal total credits for each transaction.

## Pharmacokinetics of β-blockers
β-blockers work by competitively blocking β-adrenergic receptors. β1-selective agents (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. Non-selective agents (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) also block β2, causing bronchoconstriction and reduced peripheral vasodilation. Mixed α/β blockers (carvedilol, labetalol) add α1-blockade for vasodilation.
Pharmacokinetics vary: oral bioavailability is 50% for metoprolol and atenolol, 30% for propranolol (high first-pass). Half-lives range from metoprolol 3–7 h (ER 12 h) to nebivolol 12–20 h. Atenolol, nadolol, and sotalol are renally excreted and need dose adjustment when CrCl <30 mL/min.
Typical adult doses (once-daily unless noted): metoprolol tartrate 50–100 mg bid, ER 25–200 mg; atenolol 25–100 mg; bisoprolol 1.25–10 mg; carvedilol 3.125–25 mg bid (titrate); nebivolol 2.5–20 mg; propranolol 40–160 mg tid/qid (IR) or 80–160 mg LA; sotalol 80–160 mg bid (adjust for CrCl).
Indications include hypertension, chronic stable angina, post-MI mortality reduction, HFrEF (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol-ER, nebivolol), rate control in AF/flutter, ventricular arrhythmia prophylaxis (sotalol), migraine prophylaxis (propranolol), essential tremor, and glaucoma (topical timolol).
Key: Atenolol, nadolol, and sotalol require dose adjustment in renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min).
Key: β1-selective agents lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release; non-selective agents also cause bronchoconstriction.

## Water Cycle Basics
The water cycle is a sun-driven, closed system that moves water through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and runoff/infiltration. It involves changes in state (liquid, gas, solid) and has reservoirs like oceans, ice caps, groundwater, and the atmosphere. The total mass of water stays constant; it only shifts location or state.
In contrast, the carbon cycle is a chemical cycle, not just physical state changes. Its reservoirs include rocks, fossil fuels, the ocean, the biosphere, and the atmosphere. Key processes are photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, and diffusion. These processes move carbon between reservoirs, with combustion releasing large amounts into the atmosphere.
Key: Water cycle: driven by solar energy, closed system, processes include evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff/infiltration.
Key: Carbon cycle: chemical cycle, reservoirs include rocks, fossil fuels, ocean, biosphere, atmosphere; processes include photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, diffusion.

## Carbon Cycle Basics
The water and carbon cycles are both biogeochemical processes that move essential materials around Earth, but they differ in key ways. The water cycle is driven by solar energy and involves physical changes of state—liquid, gas, and solid—with most water stored in oceans. Its main processes are evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and runoff, and it is a mostly closed system where mass stays constant.
The carbon cycle is a chemical cycle, not just a change in state. Carbon is stored in rocks, fossil fuels, the ocean, the biosphere, and the atmosphere. Key processes include photosynthesis (plants take CO2 and sunlight to make glucose and oxygen), respiration (living things break down glucose and release CO2), decomposition (dead matter releases carbon), combustion (burning releases carbon), and diffusion (exchange between ocean and air).
Key: Water cycle: physical states, solar-driven, closed system.
Key: Carbon cycle: chemical transformations, major reservoirs in rocks and oceans.
Key: Both are biogeochemical cycles essential for life.

## Bismarck's Alliance System
Bismarck secured the new German Reich by isolating France, whose defeat in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71 and loss of Alsace-Lorraine left lasting resentment. He built alliances: the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, Italy joined in 1882 to form the Triple Alliance, and the Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 kept Russia neutral.
When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse, France seized the opportunity, and the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894 threatened Germany with a war on two fronts. This danger shaped German strategy.
On land, the Schlieffen Plan, drafted in 1905 and refined by Helmuth von Moltke the Younger, committed Germany to a rapid offensive against France through Belgium. This plan was a response to the two-front threat.
The Agadir Crisis of 1911, when the German gunboat Panther appeared off the Moroccan coast, brought France and Germany to the brink of war. Earlier, in the First Moroccan Crisis of 1905-06, Wilhelm II landed at Tangier to contest French influence, and the Algeciras Conference of 1906 ended in humiliation for Germany.

## Assembly Composition and Officers
Any Delegate may introduce a bill by filing three typed copies with the Clerk of the Roll before 8:15 a.m. on a Tuesday. The Clerk assigns a number with the prefix 'BA' and the session year, and reads the title aloud at the first session after filing (First Reading), with no debate.
The Speaker refers each bill to one of four standing committees: Grounds (7 members), Clubs (7), Chest (9), or Rules (8). A bill spending more than 40 Silver Marks must go to the Committee on the Chest.
The Clerk of the Roll keeps the Ledger of Bills. The Assembly has 31 elected Delegates, the Speaker presides and votes only to break ties, and the Provost of Finance certifies spending bills. A quorum is 20 Delegates; if a quorum call fails twice in one session, the Speaker must adjourn.

## Committee Stage
A bill cannot be voted on the same day it receives its Second Reading, unless every Delegate present agrees unanimously. This rule is crucial: it prevents immediate final votes and ensures a waiting period.
After a bill is reported from committee, it gets its Second Reading at least three school days later. The Clerk reads the full text, and each Delegate may speak once for up to four minutes, while the Sponsor may speak twice.
Amendments are voted on individually by show of hands before the final vote. After amendments are settled, the Third Reading happens immediately, and passage needs a simple majority of Delegates present, but at least eleven yes votes.
Committees meet in Room 114 during the Thursday Activity Block, with a quorum of five. They can report the bill favorably, report it with amendments, table it until the next calendar month, or kill it by a two-thirds vote of members present.
After passage, the Chancellor must within five school days either sign the bill (making it an Act), veto it with a written objection of up to 150 words, or return it unsigned after five days (then it becomes an Act without signature).

## Why circular motion is special
An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating because its direction changes continuously. Velocity is a vector, so changing direction changes velocity, even if speed stays the same. This acceleration is called centripetal acceleration, and it always points toward the center of the circle, perpendicular to the velocity. It only changes direction, not speed.
The net force that produces this acceleration is the centripetal force, and it must be supplied by something real: tension in a string, friction on a tire, or gravity on a satellite. Without a real force, the object would move in a straight line.
For uniform circular motion, the speed can be found from the period T (time for one full circle) using v = 2πr / T. The centripetal acceleration is a = v² / r, and the centripetal force is F = m v² / r.

## Key formulas for uniform circular motion
In uniform circular motion, an object moves at constant speed but still accelerates because its direction changes continuously. This acceleration is centripetal, always pointing toward the circle's center, and it changes only direction, not speed.
The net force causing this acceleration is the centripetal force, and it must come from a real source: tension, friction, or gravity. Without such a real force, circular motion cannot occur.
The key formulas are: centripetal acceleration a = v²/r, centripetal force F = mv²/r, and speed from period v = 2πr/T, where T is the time for one full circle.

## Worked example: car on a flat curve
A 1200 kg car rounds a flat, unbanked curve of radius 50 m at a steady 20 m/s. Its centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r = (20 m/s)² / 50 m = 8.0 m/s². The required centripetal force is F = ma = (1200 kg)(8.0 m/s²) = 9600 N, about 9.6 kN.
This force must be supplied by friction between the tires and the road, directed toward the center of the curve. If the maximum available friction is smaller (e.g., on ice or with worn tires), the car skids outward. The skid is not due to an outward force; rather, the centripetal force is missing, so the car continues in a straight line.
A geostationary satellite orbits Earth in a circle of radius r = 4.23 × 10⁷ m with a period T = 24 h = 86,400 s. Its orbital speed is v = 2πr/T ≈ 3.08 × 10³ m/s (about 3.1 km/s). Its centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r ≈ 0.22 m/s².
Earth's gravity provides exactly this 0.22 m/s² acceleration, bending the satellite's path into a circle once per day. The satellite is in free fall—it is falling around Earth, not floating force-free.

## Centripetal force is not a new force
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it is the name for whatever real force (tension, friction, gravity, a normal force) points toward the center. Never draw a separate centripetal force arrow on a free-body diagram—identify which actual force plays that role. The centripetal force is supplied by a real interaction: friction (car on a curve), gravity (satellite), tension (ball on a string). If the required force exceeds what is available, the object leaves its circular path. The "centrifugal" push you feel in a turning car is your inertia; in an inertial frame, no outward force acts on you.

## Key formulas for uniform circular motion
In uniform circular motion, an object moves at constant speed but still accelerates because its direction changes continuously. This acceleration is centripetal, always pointing toward the circle's center, and it changes only direction, not speed.

## Centripetal force is not a new force
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it is the name for whatever real force (tension, friction, gravity, a normal force) points toward the center. Never draw a separate centripetal force arrow on a free-body diagram—identify which actual force plays that role. Uniform circular motion means constant speed but continuously changing direction, so there is always an acceleration toward the center.
The centripetal force is supplied by a real interaction: friction (car on a curve), gravity (satellite), tension (ball on a string). If the required force exceeds what is available, the object leaves its circular path. The "centrifugal" push you feel in a turning car is your inertia; in an inertial frame, no outward force acts on you.

Penicillin G is narrow-spectrum (G+ and some G-), given IV 2-4 MU q4-6h. For syphilis, penicillin is the drug of choice, but if allergic, use doxycycline. ## Cephalosporins
Cephalosporins are beta-lactam antibiotics grouped by generation. First-generation drugs like cefalexin cover MSSA, strep, and some E. coli, but they do NOT cover Pseudomonas. Second-generation cefuroxime adds H. influenzae and Moraxella, but it is also NOT anti-pseudomonal; you need a third- or fourth-generation agent for Pseudomonas. Third-generation ceftriaxone covers Neisseria and H. influenzae, but it should be avoided in hyperbilirubinemia because it can displace bilirubin. Ceftazidime is a third-generation anti-pseudomonal, but it has limited anaerobic coverage. Fourth-generation cefepime is broad and anti-pseudomonal, but it requires dose adjustment in renal failure (CrCl < 50).

## Cephalosporins
Cephalosporins are beta-lactam antibiotics grouped by generation. First-generation drugs like cefalexin cover MSSA, strep, and some E. coli, but they do NOT cover Pseudomonas. Second-generation cefuroxime adds H. influenzae and Moraxella, but it is also NOT anti-pseudomonal; you need a third- or fourth-generation agent for Pseudomonas. Third-generation ceftriaxone covers Neisseria and H. influenzae, but it should be avoided in hyperbilirubinemia because it can displace bilirubin. Ceftazidime is a third-generation anti-pseudomonal, but it has limited anaerobic coverage. Fourth-generation cefepime is broad and anti-pseudomonal, but it requires dose adjustment in renal failure (CrCl < 50).

## Fluoroquinolones
Fluoroquinolones differ: ciprofloxacin is the anti-Pseudomonal one; levofloxacin is not, and moxifloxacin is not for MRSA. Ciprofloxacin has limited activity against atypicals, so add a macrolide. Aztreonam is only for Gram-negatives, so it won't treat Gram-positive infections even in penicillin-allergic patients. Ertapenem does not cover MRSA.
Renal dosing: ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO/IV q12h, halve if CrCl<30, avoid if <15. Levofloxacin 750 mg q24h, adjust 50% if CrCl<50. Moxifloxacin 400 mg q24h, largely unchanged, caution if CrCl<30.

## Tetracyclines
Several antibiotics are safe in renal failure, but each has its own caveats. Erythromycin, clarithromycin, and azithromycin need no renal adjustment, yet they can cause GI upset and QTc prolongation. Clindamycin is also safe in renal failure but carries a risk of C. difficile colitis. Aminoglycosides are the opposite: gentamicin, tobramycin, and amikacin all require careful monitoring and dose adjustment in renal impairment, and amikacin is not safe in anuric patients without dialysis. Vancomycin also needs dose adjustment based on renal function and trough levels.
Watch for common exam traps. Clarithromycin does not treat H. pylori alone; it needs a PPI plus amoxicillin or metronidazole. Clindamycin is not first-line for strep throat; penicillin is preferred. Also, azithromycin does not cover MRSA, and doxycycline and minocycline do not cover Pseudomonas.

## Aminoglycosides
Aminoglycosides like gentamicin, tobramycin, and amikacin are for aerobic Gram-negative bacteria, not anaerobes. They require renal monitoring and dose adjustment; in stable CKD, monitoring is still essential. In anuric patients, amikacin is not safe without dialysis removal. Vancomycin covers Gram-positive bacteria, not Gram-negative.
Gentamicin dosing is 5 mg/kg IV q24h, or extended-interval 5-7 mg/kg q24h with trough monitoring. Tobramycin is similar and anti-Pseudomonal. Amikacin is 15 mg/kg IV q24h for multi-drug resistant Gram-negative. Vancomycin is 15-20 mg/kg IV q12h, adjusted to trough 15-20 µg/mL for serious infections.
All these drugs need renal dose adjustment and monitoring.

## Double-Entry Bookkeeping Fundamentals
Double-entry bookkeeping records every financial transaction in at least two accounts, ensuring the books always balance. The golden rule is that for every debit, there must be an equal and offsetting credit.
To record a transaction, first identify it: determine if cash is moving in or out and which category it belongs to (e.g., inventory purchase, sales revenue, rent expense). Then determine the two accounts affected—for example, paying for inventory with cash affects the 'Inventory' asset account and the 'Cash' asset account.
Apply the debit and credit rules using the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity): debits increase assets and expenses; credits increase liabilities, equity, and revenue. Finally, record the entry with the date, a description, the debit amount, and the credit amount in the general ledger, and verify that total debits equal total credits for each transaction.

Key: Determine the accounts: Decide which two accounts are affected.

## Lithosphere and Plate Motion
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they mark the boundaries where tectonic plates interact. The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere, moving via mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push at rates measured in centimetres per year. At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, causing normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Stress builds when plate edges lock by friction, until strain exceeds rock strength, releasing as earthquakes. Fault geometry, rheological contrasts, and curved margins also focus deformation.
Key points: Earthquakes trace plate interactions; lithosphere is rigid plates on asthenosphere; motion is cm/yr; stress accumulation from locked edges. Questions: Why are earthquakes not random? What happens at divergent boundaries? How is plate motion measured? What causes stress accumulation?

## Types of Plate Boundaries
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they outline the moving plates' framework. The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere, moving at centimetres per year. At boundaries, plates interact in three ways: divergent (pulling apart, causing normal-fault quakes at shallow depths), convergent (colliding, causing thrust-fault quakes from deep to shallow), and transform (sliding past, causing strike-slip quakes at shallow to intermediate depths).
Quakes cluster at boundaries because plate edges lock by friction, building strain until it exceeds rock strength. Fault geometry, rheological contrasts, and curved margins also focus deformation. So, the pattern of earthquakes directly reflects plate kinematics.

β-blockers work by competitively blocking β-adrenergic receptors. β1-selective agents (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. ## Pharmacokinetics of β-blockers
β-blockers work by competitively blocking β-adrenergic receptors. β1-selective agents (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. Non-selective agents (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) also block β2, causing bronchoconstriction and reduced peripheral vasodilation. Mixed α/β blockers (carvedilol, labetalol) add α1-blockade for vasodilation.
Pharmacokinetics vary: oral bioavailability is 50% for metoprolol and atenolol, 30% for propranolol (high first-pass). Half-lives range from metoprolol 3–7 h (ER 12 h) to nebivolol 12–20 h. Atenolol, nadolol, and sotalol are renally excreted and need dose adjustment when CrCl <30 mL/min.

## Dosing of β-blockers

## Drug interactions with β-blockers
In special populations, dosing and agent choice must be adjusted. For elderly patients, start with a low dose and increase slowly. In chronic kidney disease (CKD), use renally cleared agents like atenolol or nadolol, and reduce the dose. In heart failure (HF), titrate up to target doses: bisoprolol 10 mg, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, or metoprolol-ER 200 mg.
Key drug interactions: bradycardia is increased with digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem, and ivabradine. Hypotension is increased with ACE inhibitors/ARBs and diuretics. NSAIDs reduce the antihypertensive effect. CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g., fluoxetine, paroxetine) raise metoprolol levels.
Contraindications and cautions include asthma/COPD with reversible bronchospasm (avoid non-selective), sinus bradycardia <50 bpm, 2nd/3rd degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome, cardiogenic shock, decompensated HF (initiate only when euvolemic), severe peripheral arterial disease, pregnancy (avoid atenolol; labetalol preferred), and diabetes (mask hypoglycemia; prefer β1-selective or nebivolol). CYP2D6 poor metabolizers have increased metoprolol and carvedilol levels.
Monitoring includes HR, BP, ECG (PR/QRS), renal function, electrolytes (K+), glucose, and lipid profile (non-selective increase TG, decrease HDL). Adverse effects hierarchy: fatigue, cold extremities, sexual dysfunction > bronchospasm (non-selective) > hyperglycemia mask > depression (rare) > heart block. Withdrawal: taper over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound tachycardia, hypertension, ischemia.

## Water Cycle Basics
The water cycle is a sun-driven, closed system that moves water through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and runoff/infiltration. It involves changes in state (liquid, gas, solid) and has reservoirs like oceans, ice caps, groundwater, and the atmosphere. The total mass of water stays constant; it only shifts location or state.
In contrast, the carbon cycle is a chemical cycle, not just physical state changes. Its reservoirs include rocks, fossil fuels, the ocean, the biosphere, and the atmosphere. Key processes are photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, and diffusion. These processes move carbon between reservoirs, with combustion releasing large amounts into the atmosphere.
Key: Water cycle: driven by solar energy, closed system, processes include evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff/infiltration.

## Carbon Cycle Basics
The water and carbon cycles are both biogeochemical processes that move essential materials around Earth, but they differ in key ways. The water cycle is driven by solar energy and involves physical changes of state—liquid, gas, and solid—with most water stored in oceans. Its main processes are evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and runoff, and it is a mostly closed system where mass stays constant.
The carbon cycle is a chemical cycle, not just a change in state. Carbon is stored in rocks, fossil fuels, the ocean, the biosphere, and the atmosphere. Key processes include photosynthesis (plants take CO2 and sunlight to make glucose and oxygen), respiration (living things break down glucose and release CO2), decomposition (dead matter releases carbon), combustion (burning releases carbon), and diffusion (exchange between ocean and air).

## Assembly Composition and Officers
Any Delegate may introduce a bill by filing three typed copies with the Clerk of the Roll before 8:15 a.m. on a Tuesday. The Clerk assigns a number with the prefix 'BA' and the session year, and reads the title aloud at the first session after filing (First Reading), with no debate.
The Speaker refers each bill to one of four standing committees: Grounds (7 members), Clubs (7), Chest (9), or Rules (8). A bill spending more than 40 Silver Marks must go to the Committee on the Chest.
The Clerk of the Roll keeps the Ledger of Bills. The Assembly has 31 elected Delegates, the Speaker presides and votes only to break ties, and the Provost of Finance certifies spending bills. A quorum is 20 Delegates; if a quorum call fails twice in one session, the Speaker must adjourn.

Emergency measures affecting health or safety can be introduced at any session and need 24 of 31 Delegates to pass. They expire after 20 school days unless re-enacted normally.

## Scope and Definitions
The Rental Law of the Republic of Ostrava applies to all residential lease agreements made within its territory. Key definitions: a Tenant is a natural person occupying a dwelling under a written lease; a Landlord is the legal title holder or authorized manager; the Regulatory Office is the Office of Tenancy Regulation from Article 12.
The rent increase provision is important for the upcoming assessment—it will be on the test. Rent may be raised only once every 12 months, and the increase cannot exceed 5% of the prevailing rent unless the Landlord gets prior written approval from the Housing Arbitration Bureau, which requires showing capital improvements over 15% of the property's assessed value.
The Tenant must keep the interior clean and promptly notify the Landlord of any defect. If the Landlord fails to fix a reported defect within 14 days, the Tenant may reduce rent by up to 10% per month until it is cured. The Landlord is responsible for maintaining structural elements, plumbing, heating, and electrical systems in habitable condition.
Security deposits are limited to two months' rent, must be held in an escrow account by the Ministry of Urban Dwelling, and returned within 45 days after lease termination, minus lawful deductions for damage beyond normal wear. Leases must be at least 120 days unless both parties agree in writing to a shorter term, but not less than 30 days; shorter leases are void.

## Minimum Lease Term
The minimum lease term under the Rental Law of the Republic of Ostrava is 120 calendar days, unless both parties agree in writing to a shorter term, which cannot be less than 30 days. Any lease shorter than 30 days is void from the start.
Rent can be increased only once every 12 months, and the increase cannot exceed 5% of the prevailing rent unless the landlord gets prior written approval from the Housing Arbitration Bureau, which requires showing that capital improvements over 15% of the property's assessed value were completed. This provision will be on the test.
The law applies to all residential leases within the Republic of Ostrava. A tenant is a natural person under a written lease; a landlord is the title holder or authorized manager; the Regulatory Office is the Office of Tenancy Regulation under Article 12.
Security deposits are limited to two months' rent, must be held in an escrow account by the Ministry of Urban Dwelling, and returned within 45 days after lease termination, minus lawful deductions for damage beyond normal wear.
The landlord must maintain structural elements, plumbing, heating, and electrical systems in habitable condition. The tenant must keep the interior clean and promptly notify the landlord of any defect. If the landlord fails to remedy a reported defect within 14 days, the tenant may reduce rent by up to 10% per month until it is fixed.
Either party may terminate a periodic tenancy with at least 60 days' written notice before the intended termination date.

## Rent Adjustment Mechanism
The rent adjustment mechanism in the Republic of Ostrava is a key topic for the upcoming assessment, so be sure to understand it. Rent may be increased no more than once every twelve months, and the increase cannot exceed five percent of the prevailing rent. However, a larger increase is allowed if the Landlord obtains prior written approval from the Housing Arbitration Bureau, which requires demonstrating that capital improvements exceeding fifteen percent of the property's assessed value have been completed.

## Early Termination and Non-Payment
For fixed-term leases, early termination is only allowed if both parties agree in writing or if the Housing Arbitration Bureau orders it after a serious breach. A tenant may sublet or assign the lease only with the landlord's prior written consent, which cannot be unreasonably withheld. The landlord must respond within twenty business days; if they don't, consent is deemed given.
A landlord who violates Articles 3, 4, or 5 faces a fine of up to twelve percent of the annual rent per violation, paid to the Ministry of Urban Dwelling. Repeated violations within 24 months can lead to suspension of the rental license for up to 180 days.

## Bismarck's Alliance System
Bismarck secured the new German Reich by isolating France, whose defeat in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71 and loss of Alsace-Lorraine left lasting resentment. He built alliances: the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, Italy joined in 1882 to form the Triple Alliance, and the Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 kept Russia neutral.
When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse, France seized the opportunity, and the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894 threatened Germany with a war on two fronts. This danger shaped German strategy.
On land, the Schlieffen Plan, drafted in 1905 and refined by Helmuth von Moltke the Younger, committed Germany to a rapid offensive against France through Belgium. This plan was a response to the two-front threat.
The Agadir Crisis of 1911, when the German gunboat Panther appeared off the Moroccan coast, brought France and Germany to the brink of war. Earlier, in the First Moroccan Crisis of 1905-06, Wilhelm II landed at Tangier to contest French influence, and the Algeciras Conference of 1906 ended in humiliation for Germany.

## Wilhelm II's Dismissal of Bismarck and the Franco-Russian Alliance
Bismarck had built a system to isolate France after its 1870-71 defeat and loss of Alsace-Lorraine, using alliances like the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary (1879), the Triple Alliance (1882), and the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia (1887). When Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse, France seized the chance and formed the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894, which threatened Germany with a war on two fronts.
The Schlieffen Plan, drafted in 1905 and refined by Moltke the Younger, was Germany's answer: a rapid offensive against France through Belgium, aiming to knock France out quickly before turning east against Russia. This plan shaped German strategy on land.
The Agadir Crisis of 1911, when the German gunboat Panther appeared off Morocco, brought France and Germany to the brink of war. Earlier, the First Moroccan Crisis (1905-06) saw Wilhelm II land at Tangier to contest French influence, but the Algeciras Conference ended in humiliation for Germany.
Britain's Entente Cordiale with France (1904) and the Anglo-Russian Entente (1907) divided Europe into two armed camps—the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente—though these agreements had no formal military obligations. An arms race, including German naval laws and the Dreadnought, accompanied this realignment.

## The Balkan Wars and Their Consequences
The Balkan Wars of 1912-13, ended by the Treaty of London (May 1913) and the Treaty of Bucharest (August 1913), pushed the Ottoman Empire out of Europe and left Serbia larger and victorious. Austria-Hungary saw this enlarged Serbia as an existential threat.
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb tied to the Black Hand, gave Vienna its excuse. Austrian foreign minister Count Leopold von Berchtold got from Germany on 5-6 July the 'blank cheque,' an unconditional promise of support against Serbia.
The July Crisis then moved fast. Austria-Hungary sent Serbia an ultimatum on 23 July, deliberately made unacceptable; Serbia's conciliatory reply on 25 July was rejected, and partial mobilisation began. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July. Tsar Nicholas II ordered general Russian mobilisation on 30 July, despite telegrams with Wilhelm II. Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August. The Schlieffen Plan required invading Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had guaranteed by the Treaty of London of 1839. Sir Edward Grey's final warnings were ignored, and Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914.
Historians have debated responsibility since. Fritz Fischer, in 'Griff nach der Weltmacht' (1961), argued German leaders deliberately sought European domination, reopening controversy after Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles. Most accounts now stress the interaction of alliance commitments, militarism, imperial rivalry, and Balkan nationalism, where decisions of individual statesmen in summer 1914 turned a regional murder into a general European war.

## Why circular motion is special
An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating because its direction changes continuously. Velocity is a vector, so changing direction changes velocity, even if speed stays the same. This acceleration is called centripetal acceleration, and it always points toward the center of the circle, perpendicular to the velocity. It only changes direction, not speed.
The net force that produces this acceleration is the centripetal force, and it must be supplied by something real: tension in a string, friction on a tire, or gravity on a satellite. Without a real force, the object would move in a straight line.

## Key formulas for uniform circular motion
In uniform circular motion, an object moves at constant speed but still accelerates because its direction changes continuously. This acceleration is centripetal, always pointing toward the circle's center, and it changes only direction, not speed.
The net force causing this acceleration is the centripetal force, and it must come from a real source: tension, friction, or gravity. Without such a real force, circular motion cannot occur.
The key formulas are: centripetal acceleration a = v²/r, centripetal force F = mv²/r, and speed from period v = 2πr/T, where T is the time for one full circle.

## Worked example: car on a flat curve
A 1200 kg car rounds a flat, unbanked curve of radius 50 m at a steady 20 m/s. Its centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r = (20 m/s)² / 50 m = 8.0 m/s². The required centripetal force is F = ma = (1200 kg)(8.0 m/s²) = 9600 N, about 9.6 kN.
This force must be supplied by friction between the tires and the road, directed toward the center of the curve. If the maximum available friction is smaller (e.g., on ice or with worn tires), the car skids outward. The skid is not due to an outward force; rather, the centripetal force is missing, so the car continues in a straight line.
A geostationary satellite orbits Earth in a circle of radius r = 4.23 × 10⁷ m with a period T = 24 h = 86,400 s. Its orbital speed is v = 2πr/T ≈ 3.08 × 10³ m/s (about 3.1 km/s). Its centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r ≈ 0.22 m/s².
Earth's gravity provides exactly this 0.22 m/s² acceleration, bending the satellite's path into a circle once per day. The satellite is in free fall—it is falling around Earth, not floating force-free.

## Centripetal force is not a new force
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it is the name for whatever real force (tension, friction, gravity, a normal force) points toward the center. Never draw a separate centripetal force arrow on a free-body diagram—identify which actual force plays that role. The centripetal force is supplied by a real interaction: friction (car on a curve), gravity (satellite), tension (ball on a string). If the required force exceeds what is available, the object leaves its circular path. The "centrifugal" push you feel in a turning car is your inertia; in an inertial frame, no outward force acts on you.

This force must be supplied by friction between the tires and the road, directed toward the center of the curve. If the maximum available friction is smaller (e.g., on ice or with worn tires), the car skids outward. The skid is not due to an outward force; rather, the centripetal force is missing, so the car continues in a straight line.
A geostationary satellite orbits Earth in a circle of radius r = 4.23 × 10⁷ m with a period T = 24 h = 86,400 s. Its orbital speed is v = 2πr/T ≈ 3.08 × 10³ m/s (about 3.1 km/s). Its centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r ≈ 0.22 m/s².
Earth's gravity provides exactly this 0.22 m/s² acceleration, bending the satellite's path into a circle once per day. The satellite is in free fall—it is falling around Earth, not floating force-free.

## Centripetal force is not a new force

First-generation drugs like cefalexin cover MSSA, strep, and some E. coli, but they do NOT cover Pseudomonas. Second-generation cefuroxime adds H. influenzae and Moraxella, but it is also NOT anti-pseudomonal; you need a third- or fourth-generation agent for Pseudomonas. Third-generation ceftriaxone covers Neisseria and H. influenzae, but it should be avoided in hyperbilirubinemia because it can displace bilirubin. Ceftazidime is a third-generation anti-pseudomonal, but it has limited anaerobic coverage. Fourth-generation cefepime is broad and anti-pseudomonal, but it requires dose adjustment in renal failure (CrCl < 50).
Several exam traps involve penicillin-related drugs. Penicillin is the drug of choice for syphilis, but if allergic, use doxycycline. Amoxicillin alone does NOT cover MRSA; you need an add-on. Flucloxacillin is anti-staphylococcal (MSSA) and is NOT for Gram-negative infections. Co-amoxiclav is NOT safe in penicillin allergy due to cross-reactivity risk. Meropenem, a carbapenem, does NOT cover MRSA; you need a glycopeptide or oxazolidinone.
For renal dosing: first-generation cephalosporins (cefalexin) halve the dose if CrCl < 30. Ceftriaxone needs minimal adjustment except in severe renal impairment. Cefepime requires dose reduction and extended interval if CrCl < 50.

## Glycopeptides
Several exam traps warn against common misconceptions. Gentamicin must be monitored even in stable CKD; tobramycin does not cover anaerobes; amikacin is not safe in anuric patients without dialysis removal; vancomycin does not cover Gram-negative bacteria; teicoplanin requires renal adjustment; linezolid needs CBC monitoring in renal failure; tedizolid still requires avoiding serotonergic agents; co-trimoxazole does not treat all community-acquired pneumonia due to limited streptococcal coverage; and metronidazole does not cover aerobic Gram-negatives.
For aminoglycosides, gentamicin and tobramycin target aerobic Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas, with major renal dose reduction and trough monitoring (gentamicin trough <1 µg/mL). Amikacin is used for multi-drug resistant Gram-negatives, with cautious dosing and therapeutic drug monitoring.

Linezolid and tedizolid are oxazolidinones for Gram-positive infections. Linezolid can cause myelosuppression after 2-3 weeks and serotonin syndrome with SSRIs; monitor CBC. Tedizolid has less myelosuppression but still avoid concurrent serotonergic agents.
Co-trimoxazole covers some Gram-positives and Gram-negatives (UTI, PCP), but not all CAP. Reduce TMP dose if CrCl<30. Metronidazole covers anaerobes and protozoa, with no renal adjustment (hepatic), but not aerobic Gram-negatives.

## Double-Entry Bookkeeping Fundamentals
Double-entry bookkeeping records every financial transaction in at least two accounts, ensuring the books always balance. The golden rule is that for every debit, there must be an equal and offsetting credit.
To record a transaction, first identify it: determine if cash is moving in or out and which category it belongs to (e.g., inventory purchase, sales revenue, rent expense). Then determine the two accounts affected—for example, paying for inventory with cash affects the 'Inventory' asset account and the 'Cash' asset account.
Apply the debit and credit rules using the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity): debits increase assets and expenses; credits increase liabilities, equity, and revenue. Finally, record the entry with the date, a description, the debit amount, and the credit amount in the general ledger, and verify that total debits equal total credits for each transaction.

## Lithosphere and Plate Motion
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they mark the boundaries where tectonic plates interact. The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere, moving via mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push at rates measured in centimetres per year. At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, causing normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. Stress builds when plate edges lock by friction, until strain exceeds rock strength, releasing as earthquakes. Fault geometry, rheological contrasts, and curved margins also focus deformation.
Key points: Earthquakes trace plate interactions; lithosphere is rigid plates on asthenosphere; motion is cm/yr; stress accumulation from locked edges. Questions: Why are earthquakes not random? What happens at divergent boundaries? How is plate motion measured? What causes stress accumulation?

## Types of Plate Boundaries
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they outline the moving plates' framework. The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere, moving at centimetres per year. At boundaries, plates interact in three ways: divergent (pulling apart, causing normal-fault quakes at shallow depths), convergent (colliding, causing thrust-fault quakes from deep to shallow), and transform (sliding past, causing strike-slip quakes at shallow to intermediate depths).
Quakes cluster at boundaries because plate edges lock by friction, building strain until it exceeds rock strength. Fault geometry, rheological contrasts, and curved margins also focus deformation. So, the pattern of earthquakes directly reflects plate kinematics.

## Why Earthquakes Cluster at Boundaries
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. This means their locations follow the movement patterns of tectonic plates, which is why they cluster at boundaries.
At plate boundaries, stress accumulates because plate edges are locked by friction. Strain builds until it exceeds rock strength, then earthquakes occur. This is a key reason for clustering.

## Plate Speed and Earthquake Frequency
Faster plate motion means more frequent large earthquakes. The Pacific Plate moves at about 5 cm/yr, and the Nazca Plate at about 8 cm/yr; these speeds drive the high frequency of large quakes along the Ring of Fire.
Earthquake depths vary by setting: shallow events (≤10 km) dominate divergent ridges and transform faults, while intermediate-to-deep events (30–300 km) occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone of subducting slabs. A typical subduction quake at 30 km depth releases energy from both crustal bending and slab dehydration.
The seismic cycle at a convergent margin has four phases: interseismic (strain accumulates, decades to centuries), coseismic (sudden slip releases energy, seconds to minutes), postseismic (afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation, months to years), and preseismic (possible foreshocks or slow slip).
Seismic gap theory says segments that have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events. GPS and InSAR monitor plate-scale velocities (cm/yr) to refine coupling models.

## Seismic Cycle at Convergent Margins

## Water Cycle Basics
The water cycle is a sun-driven, closed system that moves water through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and runoff/infiltration. It involves changes in state (liquid, gas, solid) and has reservoirs like oceans, ice caps, groundwater, and the atmosphere. The total mass of water stays constant; it only shifts location or state.
In contrast, the carbon cycle is a chemical cycle, not just physical state changes. Its reservoirs include rocks, fossil fuels, the ocean, the biosphere, and the atmosphere. Key processes are photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, and diffusion. These processes move carbon between reservoirs, with combustion releasing large amounts into the atmosphere.
Key: Water cycle: driven by solar energy, closed system, processes include evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff/infiltration.
Key: Carbon cycle: chemical cycle, reservoirs include rocks, fossil fuels, ocean, biosphere, atmosphere; processes include photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, diffusion.

## Carbon Cycle Basics
The water and carbon cycles are both biogeochemical processes that move essential materials around Earth, but they differ in key ways. The water cycle is driven by solar energy and involves physical changes of state—liquid, gas, and solid—with most water stored in oceans. Its main processes are evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and runoff, and it is a mostly closed system where mass stays constant.
The carbon cycle is a chemical cycle, not just a change in state. Carbon is stored in rocks, fossil fuels, the ocean, the biosphere, and the atmosphere. Key processes include photosynthesis (plants take CO2 and sunlight to make glucose and oxygen), respiration (living things break down glucose and release CO2), decomposition (dead matter releases carbon), combustion (burning releases carbon), and diffusion (exchange between ocean and air).

## Mechanism of β-blockers
β-blockers work by competitively blocking β-adrenergic receptors. β1-selective agents (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. Non-selective agents (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) also block β2 receptors, causing bronchoconstriction and reduced vasodilation. Mixed α/β blockers (carvedilol, labetalol) add α1-blockade, leading to vasodilation.
Indications include hypertension, chronic stable angina, post-MI mortality reduction, HFrEF (with bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol-ER, nebivolol), rate control in AF/flutter, ventricular arrhythmia prophylaxis (sotalol), migraine prophylaxis (propranolol), essential tremor, and glaucoma (topical timolol).

## Pharmacokinetics of β-blockers
β-blockers work by competitively blocking β-adrenergic receptors. β1-selective agents (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. Non-selective agents (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) also block β2, causing bronchoconstriction and reduced peripheral vasodilation. Mixed α/β blockers (carvedilol, labetalol) add α1-blockade for vasodilation.
Pharmacokinetics vary: oral bioavailability is 50% for metoprolol and atenolol, 30% for propranolol (high first-pass). Half-lives range from metoprolol 3–7 h (ER 12 h) to nebivolol 12–20 h. Atenolol, nadolol, and sotalol are renally excreted and need dose adjustment when CrCl <30 mL/min.
Typical adult doses (once-daily unless noted): metoprolol tartrate 50–100 mg bid, ER 25–200 mg; atenolol 25–100 mg; bisoprolol 1.25–10 mg; carvedilol 3.125–25 mg bid (titrate); nebivolol 2.5–20 mg; propranolol 40–160 mg tid/qid (IR) or 80–160 mg LA; sotalol 80–160 mg bid (adjust for CrCl).
Indications include hypertension, chronic stable angina, post-MI mortality reduction, HFrEF (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol-ER, nebivolol), rate control in AF/flutter, ventricular arrhythmia prophylaxis (sotalol), migraine prophylaxis (propranolol), essential tremor, and glaucoma (topical timolol).
Key: Atenolol, nadolol, and sotalol require dose adjustment in renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min).
Key: β1-selective agents lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release; non-selective agents also cause bronchoconstriction.
Key: Oral bioavailability: metoprolol 50%, atenolol 50%, propranolol 30% (high first-pass).
Key: Half-lives: metoprolol 3–7 h (ER 12 h), bisoprolol 10–12 h, carvedilol 7–10 h, nebivolol 12–20 h.
Key: Typical adult doses: metoprolol tartrate 50–100 mg bid, atenolol 25–100 mg, bisoprolol 1.25–10 mg, carvedilol 3.125–25 mg bid, nebivolol 2.5–20 mg, propranolol 40–160 mg tid/qid, sotalol 80–160 mg bid

## Indications for β-blockers
β-blockers are used for hypertension, chronic stable angina, reducing mortality after a heart attack, and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) using specific agents: bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol-ER, and nebivolol. They also control heart rate in atrial fibrillation/flutter, prevent ventricular arrhythmias (sotalol), and prevent migraines (propranolol).
Typical adult doses are usually once-daily unless noted. For example, metoprolol tartrate is 50–100 mg twice daily, while metoprolol ER is 25–200 mg once daily. Atenolol is 25–100 mg once daily, bisoprolol 1.25–10 mg once daily, carvedilol 3.125–25 mg twice daily (titrated), nebivolol 2.5–20 mg once daily, propranolol 40–160 mg three or four times daily (or 80–160 mg long-acting), and sotalol 80–160 mg twice daily (adjusted for kidney function).

## Assembly Composition and Officers
Any Delegate may introduce a bill by filing three typed copies with the Clerk of the Roll before 8:15 a.m. on a Tuesday. The Clerk assigns a number with the prefix 'BA' and the session year, and reads the title aloud at the first session after filing (First Reading), with no debate.

## Committee Stage
A bill cannot be voted on the same day it receives its Second Reading, unless every Delegate present agrees unanimously. This rule is crucial: it prevents immediate final votes and ensures a waiting period.

Amendments are voted on individually by show of hands before the final vote. After amendments are settled, the Third Reading happens immediately, and passage needs a simple majority of Delegates present, but at least eleven yes votes.

## Minimum Lease Term
The minimum lease term under the Rental Law of the Republic of Ostrava is 120 calendar days, unless both parties agree in writing to a shorter term, which cannot be less than 30 days. Any lease shorter than 30 days is void from the start.
Rent can be increased only once every 12 months, and the increase cannot exceed 5% of the prevailing rent unless the landlord gets prior written approval from the Housing Arbitration Bureau, which requires showing that capital improvements over 15% of the property's assessed value were completed. This provision will be on the test.
The law applies to all residential leases within the Republic of Ostrava. A tenant is a natural person under a written lease; a landlord is the title holder or authorized manager; the Regulatory Office is the Office of Tenancy Regulation under Article 12.
Security deposits are limited to two months' rent, must be held in an escrow account by the Ministry of Urban Dwelling, and returned within 45 days after lease termination, minus lawful deductions for damage beyond normal wear.
The landlord must maintain structural elements, plumbing, heating, and electrical systems in habitable condition. The tenant must keep the interior clean and promptly notify the landlord of any defect. If the landlord fails to remedy a reported defect within 14 days, the tenant may reduce rent by up to 10% per month until it is fixed.
Either party may terminate a periodic tenancy with at least 60 days' written notice before the intended termination date.

## Why circular motion is special
An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating because its direction changes continuously. Velocity is a vector, so changing direction changes velocity, even if speed stays the same. This acceleration is called centripetal acceleration, and it always points toward the center of the circle, perpendicular to the velocity. It only changes direction, not speed.
The net force that produces this acceleration is the centripetal force, and it must be supplied by something real: tension in a string, friction on a tire, or gravity on a satellite. Without a real force, the object would move in a straight line.
For uniform circular motion, the speed can be found from the period T (time for one full circle) using v = 2πr / T. The centripetal acceleration is a = v² / r, and the centripetal force is F = m v² / r.

## Key formulas for uniform circular motion
In uniform circular motion, an object moves at constant speed but still accelerates because its direction changes continuously. This acceleration is centripetal, always pointing toward the circle's center, and it changes only direction, not speed.
The net force causing this acceleration is the centripetal force, and it must come from a real source: tension, friction, or gravity. Without such a real force, circular motion cannot occur.
The key formulas are: centripetal acceleration a = v²/r, centripetal force F = mv²/r, and speed from period v = 2πr/T, where T is the time for one full circle.

## Worked example: car on a flat curve
A 1200 kg car rounds a flat, unbanked curve of radius 50 m at a steady 20 m/s. Its centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r = (20 m/s)² / 50 m = 8.0 m/s². The required centripetal force is F = ma = (1200 kg)(8.0 m/s²) = 9600 N, about 9.6 kN.
This force must be supplied by friction between the tires and the road, directed toward the center of the curve. If the maximum available friction is smaller (e.g., on ice or with worn tires), the car skids outward. The skid is not due to an outward force; rather, the centripetal force is missing, so the car continues in a straight line.
A geostationary satellite orbits Earth in a circle of radius r = 4.23 × 10⁷ m with a period T = 24 h = 86,400 s. Its orbital speed is v = 2πr/T ≈ 3.08 × 10³ m/s (about 3.1 km/s). Its centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r ≈ 0.22 m/s².
Earth's gravity provides exactly this 0.22 m/s² acceleration, bending the satellite's path into a circle once per day. The satellite is in free fall—it is falling around Earth, not floating force-free.

## Centripetal force is not a new force
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it is the name for whatever real force (tension, friction, gravity, a normal force) points toward the center. ## Key formulas for uniform circular motion
In uniform circular motion, an object moves at constant speed but still accelerates because its direction changes continuously. This acceleration is centripetal, always pointing toward the circle's center, and it changes only direction, not speed.
The net force causing this acceleration is the centripetal force, and it must come from a real source: tension, friction, or gravity.
The key formulas are: centripetal acceleration a = v²/r, centripetal force F = mv²/r, and speed from period v = 2πr/T, where T is the time for one full circle.

A 1200 kg car rounds a flat, unbanked curve of radius 50 m at a steady 20 m/s. Its centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r = (20 m/s)² / 50 m = 8.0 m/s².

## Centripetal force is not a new force
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it is the name for whatever real force (tension, friction, gravity, a normal force) points toward the center. Never draw a separate centripetal force arrow on a free-body diagram—identify which actual force plays that role. Uniform circular motion means constant speed but continuously changing direction, so there is always an acceleration toward the center.
The centripetal force is supplied by a real interaction: friction (car on a curve), gravity (satellite), tension (ball on a string). If the required force exceeds what is available, the object leaves its circular path. The "centrifugal" push you feel in a turning car is your inertia; in an inertial frame, no outward force acts on you.

## Bismarck's Alliance System
Bismarck secured the new German Reich by isolating France, whose defeat in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71 and loss of Alsace-Lorraine left lasting resentment. He built alliances: the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, Italy joined in 1882 to form the Triple Alliance, and the Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 kept Russia neutral.
When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse, France seized the opportunity, and the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894 threatened Germany with a war on two fronts. This danger shaped German strategy.
On land, the Schlieffen Plan, drafted in 1905 and refined by Helmuth von Moltke the Younger, committed Germany to a rapid offensive against France through Belgium. This plan was a response to the two-front threat.
The Agadir Crisis of 1911, when the German gunboat Panther appeared off the Moroccan coast, brought France and Germany to the brink of war. Earlier, in the First Moroccan Crisis of 1905-06, Wilhelm II landed at Tangier to contest French influence, and the Algeciras Conference of 1906 ended in humiliation for Germany.

Bismarck, the German Chancellor, aimed to secure the new Reich by isolating France, which resented its defeat in the Franco-Prussian War and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine. This danger led to the Schlieffen Plan, drafted in 1905 and refined by Moltke the Younger, which committed Germany to a rapid offensive against France through Belgium.

## Wilhelm II's Dismissal of Bismarck and the Franco-Russian Alliance
Bismarck had built a system to isolate France after its 1870-71 defeat and loss of Alsace-Lorraine, using alliances like the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary (1879), the Triple Alliance (1882), and the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia (1887). When Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse, France seized the chance and formed the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894, which threatened Germany with a war on two fronts.
The Schlieffen Plan, drafted in 1905 and refined by Moltke the Younger, was Germany's answer: a rapid offensive against France through Belgium, aiming to knock France out quickly before turning east against Russia. This plan shaped German strategy on land.
The Agadir Crisis of 1911, when the German gunboat Panther appeared off Morocco, brought France and Germany to the brink of war. Earlier, the First Moroccan Crisis (1905-06) saw Wilhelm II land at Tangier to contest French influence, but the Algeciras Conference ended in humiliation for Germany.
Britain's Entente Cordiale with France (1904) and the Anglo-Russian Entente (1907) divided Europe into two armed camps—the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente—though these agreements had no formal military obligations. An arms race, including German naval laws and the Dreadnought, accompanied this realignment.

## The Balkan Wars and Their Consequences
The Balkan Wars of 1912-13, ended by the Treaty of London (May 1913) and the Treaty of Bucharest (August 1913), pushed the Ottoman Empire out of Europe and left Serbia larger and victorious. Austria-Hungary saw this enlarged Serbia as an existential threat.
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb tied to the Black Hand, gave Vienna its excuse. Austrian foreign minister Count Leopold von Berchtold got from Germany on 5-6 July the 'blank cheque,' an unconditional promise of support against Serbia.
The July Crisis then moved fast. Austria-Hungary sent Serbia an ultimatum on 23 July, deliberately made unacceptable; Serbia's conciliatory reply on 25 July was rejected, and partial mobilisation began. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July. Tsar Nicholas II ordered general Russian mobilisation on 30 July, despite telegrams with Wilhelm II. Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August. The Schlieffen Plan required invading Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had guaranteed by the Treaty of London of 1839. Sir Edward Grey's final warnings were ignored, and Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914.
Historians have debated responsibility since. Fritz Fischer, in 'Griff nach der Weltmacht' (1961), argued German leaders deliberately sought European domination, reopening controversy after Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles. Most accounts now stress the interaction of alliance commitments, militarism, imperial rivalry, and Balkan nationalism, where decisions of individual statesmen in summer 1914 turned a regional murder into a general European war.
